Given the volume, only the freshest 1-2 day-decay items (from 2026-10-26/10-27 records, 17 candidates: The Helpful Agent Problem, Phronix, Don't Forget What You Just Learned, Understanding Communication Failures in MAS, Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model, Trust-Agreement Gap, SPECMEM, Toolflation, AgentTriage, UniGuard, Herding and Runaway Cascades, Chair Personas, Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents, Auditing Behavioral Detectors, Handshake Overhead, RoleFlow, Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness) were individually re-compared against today's selected trio; none matched or exceeded the direction value of the task-success-blind-spot theme, so none were pulled forward. Deeper-decay items (3-14 days) were not individually re-scored this run given the unusually large fresh Layer A/B pool already yielding a strong, well-evidenced selection; this is a scope limitation to flag for tomorrow's run if the pattern repeats with another oversized batch.

toolDegradation: Semantic Scholar: both mcp__groundlane__paper_lookup and direct https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/... returned persistent RATE_LIMITED/429 across every attempt (SABench, CRM-Agent-Bench, iPrefBench, and all background-signal checks). Substituted with: arXiv API comment-field venue statements (self-reported by authors, cross-checked against the paper's own text), HuggingFace Daily Papers upvote counts, and GitHub stars via img.shields.io. Citation counts for all three selected papers are inferred as 'effectively none yet' from publication recency (2-5 days old) rather than measured directly.

arxiv.org/list pages: full-page web_fetch (format=text, extract=full) hit an upstream OUTPUT_LIMIT error on cs.AI/new and cs.CL/new default page sizes (711 and 374 total entries including cross-lists/replacements). Worked around by paginating with ?skip=N&show=25 and, for most pages, switching to mcp__groundlane__web_extract with CSS selectors (.list-title / a[href*='/abs/']) to pull titles and ids separately. Caveat: on at least one page (cs.AI skip=50) the title-list and id-list arrays were misaligned by one position relative to each other (confirmed by cross-checking 3 ids against the arXiv export API, which returned different papers than the title-based guess for ids 2610.34425, 2609.23056, and 2610.34185). All candidate ids actually logged in this record were re-verified against their expected titles via a direct arXiv export API id_list query before being written here; any title/id pairing from the raw selector scan that was not re-verified this way was not used to assign a specific id in this record.

candidates.title: Task Success Is Not Enough: Side-effect-Aware Evaluation of Tool-Using Language Model Agents
candidates.venue: NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track, accepted per author arXiv comment field)
candidates.citationVelocity: published 3 days ago; Semantic Scholar persistently 429, presumed ~0 given timing
candidates.institution: Macao Polytechnic University + Southwest Medical University + Netherlands Cancer Institute + Radboud University Medical Center
communitySignals: HF paper page exists, 1 HF dataset citing it (the released sabench dataset)
not seen in this run's HF Daily Papers trending scan
credibilityEvidence: Section 5-6: 2,211 model-task pairs across 11 frontier LLMs, template-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs
Appendix A.9: blinded 3-annotator human audit agrees with oracle on 72/78 decisive writes (92.3%)
Appendix A.8/A.10: ablations on alternative authorization/visibility policies and a prompt-level mitigation study
Section 9 Limitations: explicit, non-overclaiming scope statement
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers problem formulation, deterministic oracle design, 11-model main results, 5 named failure-mode breakdowns, and a mitigation ablation; each model-task pair run only once limits variance estimates to template composition rather than sampling noise
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The bounded claim (task success rate does not reflect authorization-boundary violations in this office-tool setting) is directly supported by the paired statistics and the independent human audit
candidates.primaryLimitation: Scoped to three office-tool domains (email/calendar/ticket); each model-task pair ran once; not yet validated for coding-agent or robotic-agent collateral damage
candidates.presentationReason: Method, oracle formalization, experimental setup, and limitations are all explicitly and precisely stated with formal notation
candidates.reason: Selected as the clearest, most rigorously evidenced instance of today's theme (task-success metrics hiding a distinct failure mode): a NeurIPS-accepted, fully open-sourced deterministic-oracle benchmark with human-audited claims.

candidates.title: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments
candidates.citationVelocity: published 5 days ago; Semantic Scholar persistently 429, presumed ~0 given timing
credibilityEvidence: Section 4: 555 strictly-conjunctive-contract tasks, 16-system comparison with per-domain and per-check breakdowns
Appendix C (summarized in Section 4.1): 3-round reliability study with Spearman rank correlations 0.869-0.934 and task-level flip-rate analysis
Section 4.2/4.4: explicit response-only-vs-strict (10.5-11.0pt) and negative-check-vs-full-contract (91.2% vs 66.8%) gap quantification
Table 1: systematic related-work comparison against 11 other benchmarks on 8 evaluation properties
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers outcome/trajectory/cost/policy-compliance as four separately reported facets with concrete breakdowns and a 3-round reliability check, though that reliability check covers only part of the full 16-system set and the main leaderboard is single-round
reproducibilityEvidence: GitHub: https://github.com/salesforce-misc/crm-agent-bench (self-contained, synthetic data, no live CRM backend required)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Both bounded claims (response-only overestimates strict success; avoiding forbidden actions is not the same as full-contract compliance) are backed by explicit, specific percentages rather than qualitative description
candidates.primaryLimitation: Built and evaluated entirely by a single vendor (Salesforce) that itself sells CRM software; although the model roster spans the whole market (Gemini/Claude/GPT/open-weight) rather than only Salesforce's own product, independent third-party replication is still pending, and the 3-round reliability study shows 30/555 task outcomes flip across rounds for the top model
candidates.presentationReason: The four-facet framing, contract check-family taxonomy, and reporting protocol are explained with explicit formulas and a worked example (Figure 1's duplicated-checkout case)
candidates.reason: Selected as the enterprise-deployment angle of today's theme: strongest available quantification of 'saying vs. doing' for a widely-deployed vertical (CRM), with full open-source artifacts and an unusually candid 3-round noise disclosure that most vendor-authored benchmarks omit.

candidates.title: iPrefBench: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personalized Mobile Use Agents
candidates.citationVelocity: published 2 days ago; Semantic Scholar persistently 429, presumed ~0 given timing
candidates.institution: The Ohio State University + Apple (first author's internship work)
communitySignals: no GitHub/dataset release link found in the paper
credibilityEvidence: Section 3.3: 3-stage task-authoring pipeline with two rounds of human expert review per task
Section 4.5: LLM-judge-vs-human agreement kappa 0.82-0.94 across rubric/success/recall/precision judgments, cross-validated with a second judge model
Section 4.5: user-simulator fidelity check, 96.6% of answers in-character and non-volunteering
Section 4.4: two further ablations (clarification prompting, history-exposure amount) with internally consistent, non-cherry-picked tradeoffs reported (precision drop alongside recall gain)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers main results on 7 models, 3 perturbation subsets, a 4-category manual error taxonomy, and 2 additional factor analyses; limited by small task count (130) and single persona, which the paper itself flags
reproducibilityEvidence: No code, task-corpus, or environment-configuration link found anywhere in the fetched full text
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The bounded claim (action completion substantially exceeds personalized task success, concentrated in ask-only information) is supported by a full quantitative breakdown and a validated judge/simulator pipeline, even though artifacts are not yet public
candidates.primaryLimitation: Only 130 tasks, a single persona (Jordan Avery), and 7 evaluated models; the personalization ground truth and the LLM judge/user-simulator all derive from the same author-built pipeline, and no reproducible release has been found yet
candidates.presentationReason: The infer-vs-ask distinction, task design, and metric definitions (recall/precision over ask-only requirements) are given precise formal definitions and worked examples
candidates.reason: Selected as the consumer-personalization angle of today's theme, and the only candidate explicitly isolating 'inferable from history' vs. 'ask-only' as the mechanism behind the success-rate gap; distinct enough from the authorization (SABench) and policy-compliance (CRM-Agent-Bench) angles to avoid redundancy within the selected trio.
